q: In ER modelling, aggregation is used to
options: compute the sum of an attribute
treat a relationship set as an abstract entity so that it can take part in another relationship
merge two entity sets into one table
convert a weak entity into a strong entity
exp: Aggregation abstracts a relationship (with its participating entities) into a higher-level entity that can participate in further relationships.

q: Employee(eid, name, did) has a foreign key did referencing Dept(did). An attempt to insert an employee whose did does not exist in Dept will be
options: accepted and the Dept table updated automatically
accepted with did set to NULL silently
accepted only for the first such row
rejected because it violates referential integrity
exp: A non-NULL foreign key value must match an existing parent key; otherwise the DBMS rejects the insert.
Division returns A-values paired with every B in S: a1 (b1,b2) and a3 (b1,b2) qualify; a2 has only b1.

q: S(dept, gender) = (CS,M), (CS,F), (CS,M), (EE,M), (EE,M). How many rows are returned by SELECT dept, gender, COUNT(*) FROM S GROUP BY dept, gender?
exp: The distinct (dept, gender) combinations are (CS,M), (CS,F) and (EE,M): 3 groups.

q: R(A,B,C,D,E,F) has FDs AB → C, BC → AD, D → E, CF → B. The closure {A, B}+ is
exp: AB → C gives ABC; BC → AD adds D; D → E adds E. F is never derived, so the closure is {A, B, C, D, E}.

q: Which SQL statement sets an intermediate point within a transaction to which one can later roll back partially?
exp: SAVEPOINT marks a point in the transaction; ROLLBACK TO savepoint undoes only later changes.

q: For three transactions T1, T2 and T3, the number of possible serial schedules is
exp: Serial schedules correspond to orderings of the transactions: 3! = 6.

q: A drawback of creating many indexes on a table is that
options: INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE operations become slower because indexes must be maintained
SELECT queries can never use them
the table can no longer have a primary key
exp: Indexes speed up reads but add overhead on every data modification and consume extra storage.

q: The data dictionary (system catalog) of a DBMS stores
options: metadata, i.e. data about the data such as table, column and constraint definitions
exp: The catalog holds metadata: schema definitions, constraints, indexes and authorizations.

q:
Statement I: Many NoSQL systems always provide full ACID transactions across the whole cluster.
Statement II: Many NoSQL systems offer eventual consistency to gain availability and scalability.
options: Statement I is true and Statement II is false
Statement I is false and Statement II is true
exp: Many distributed NoSQL stores relax strict ACID and offer eventual consistency (BASE), so I is false and II is true.

q: In a data warehouse, a fact table typically contains
options: numeric measures (such as sales amount) and foreign keys to dimension tables
only the primary keys of source systems
exp: Fact tables store measurable quantities at a chosen granularity, together with keys linking to the dimension tables.

q: Which of the following learning methods requires class-labelled training data?
exp: Decision trees are supervised; K-means, DBSCAN and Apriori work without class labels.

q: Adding a new attribute to a table in the conceptual schema without having to rewrite existing application programs that use views is an example of
exp: Logical data independence is the capacity to change the conceptual schema without changing external schemas or application programs.

q: T(c) = A, B, A, C, B. What does SELECT c FROM T GROUP BY c HAVING COUNT(*) > 1; return?
exp: A appears twice, B twice and C once; only A and B have count above 1.

q:
Emp(eid, did) = (1,10), (2,20), (3,NULL); Dept(did, dname) = (10,X), (20,Y), (30,Z). How many rows does this return?
SELECT * FROM Emp e LEFT JOIN Dept d ON e.did = d.did WHERE d.did IS NULL;
exp: LEFT JOIN keeps all 3 employees; only employee 3 has a NULL did and finds no match, giving d.did NULL. So 1 row.

q: R(A, B, C) has FDs AB → C and C → B. R is decomposed into R1(A, C) and R2(C, B). Which statement is correct?
options: The decomposition is lossy and dependency preserving
The decomposition is lossless but not dependency preserving
The decomposition is lossy and not dependency preserving
The decomposition is lossless and dependency preserving
exp: R1 ∩ R2 = C and C → B, so C is a key of R2: lossless. But AB → C cannot be derived from the FDs of R1 and R2, so it is not dependency preserving.

q: When a multivalued attribute of an entity is converted to the relational model, it is represented by
options: a separate relation containing the entity's key and the attribute
exp: A multivalued attribute becomes a new relation with the owner's primary key plus the attribute, one row per value.

q: The relational model of data was proposed by
exp: E. F. Codd proposed the relational model in 1970; Peter Chen introduced the ER model.

q: R(A, B) = {(1,x), (2,y)} and S(B, C) = {(x,p), (z,q)}. How many tuples of R left outer join S contain a NULL?
exp: The result is (1,x,p) and (2,y,NULL). Only the tuple for (2,y) has a NULL, so 1.

q:
Match the SQL statements with their categories.
1. CREATE  2. INSERT  3. GRANT  4. COMMIT
P. DCL  Q. TCL  R. DDL  S. DML
exp: CREATE is DDL, INSERT is DML, GRANT is DCL and COMMIT is TCL.

q:
Dept(did) = 10, 20, 30; Emp(eid, did) = (1,10), (2,10), (3,30). What does this return?
SELECT did FROM Dept d WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT * FROM Emp e WHERE e.did = d.did);
exp: Departments 10 and 30 have employees. Only department 20 has no matching Emp row, so NOT EXISTS is true for it.

q: Converting a 2NF relation to 3NF involves eliminating
options: transitive dependencies of non-prime attributes on the key
exp: 2NF already removes partial dependencies; 3NF removes transitive dependencies of non-prime attributes on candidate keys.

q: Transaction T1 runs SELECT COUNT(*) FROM P WHERE age > 30 twice. In between, T2 inserts a new row with age 40 and commits, so T1 sees different counts. This anomaly is called
exp: A phantom read occurs when a repeated range query returns new rows inserted by another committed transaction.

q: In multiple-granularity locking, an intention-exclusive (IX) lock on a table means that the transaction
options: intends to set exclusive locks on some rows within the table
has locked the whole table exclusively
only wants to read the table
exp: IX indicates an intention to take X locks at a finer level (rows) below this node; it does not itself lock the whole table.

q: In a specialization, if an entity can belong to more than one lower-level entity set at the same time (e.g. a person who is both a student and an employee), the specialization is
exp: Overlapping specialization allows an entity in several sub-classes; disjoint allows at most one.

q: R(A, B, C) has primary key A and tuples (1,2,3), (2,2,3), (3,NULL,4). Which insertion will be accepted?
exp: (1,9,9) and (2,2,3) duplicate existing key values and (NULL,1,1) has a NULL key. (4,2,3) has a new non-null key, so it is accepted.
π_A(R) = {1,2,3} (3 tuples) and π_B(R) = {2,3} (2 tuples), so the product has 3 × 2 = 6 tuples.

q: Marks(sid, sub, m) = (1,M,80), (1,P,70), (2,M,60), (2,P,90), (3,M,50). What does SELECT sid FROM Marks GROUP BY sid HAVING AVG(m) > 70 return?
exp: Averages: sid 1 = 75, sid 2 = 75, sid 3 = 50. Sids 1 and 2 exceed 70.

q: R(A, B, C, D) has FDs A → B and C → D, with AC as the only key. Using the 3NF synthesis algorithm, the minimum number of relations in the decomposition is
exp: Relations (A,B) and (C,D) come from the FDs; neither contains the key AC, so a third relation (A,C) is added: 3.

q: A schedule is recoverable if
options: a transaction that reads data written by another transaction commits only after that other transaction commits
every transaction commits immediately after it starts
no two transactions access the same item
exp: Recoverability requires that if Tj reads from Ti then Ti commits before Tj, so a commit never depends on an uncommitted write.

q: According to Thomas' write rule in timestamp ordering, if TS(T) < W-TS(X) and T attempts to write X, the system
options: ignores the obsolete write and lets T continue
exp: Thomas' write rule skips outdated writes instead of aborting the transaction, increasing concurrency.

q: A secondary index on a non-ordering field of a file must be a dense index because
options: the data file is not ordered on that field, so one entry is needed for every record (or value)
secondary indexes are always smaller than primary indexes
sparse indexes cannot be stored on disk
exp: Without physical ordering on the indexed field, a sparse index cannot locate records, so every record needs an entry (or pointer).

q: For the M:N relationship set between entity sets E1 and E2, the primary key of the relationship's relation consists of
options: the primary key of E1 only
the union of the primary keys of E1 and E2
the primary key of E2 only
exp: In an M:N relationship a pair of entity instances identifies a relationship instance, so the combined keys form the key.

q: Relation R(A, B, C) has A as its only candidate key. Which of the following sets of attributes is NOT a superkey?
exp: A superkey must contain a candidate key. {B, C} lacks A, so it is not a superkey.

q: Given Enrolled(sid, cid), which expression returns the sids of students who took BOTH C1 and C2?
exp: A single tuple cannot have two cid values, so the AND selection is empty. Intersecting the sids for C1 and C2 gives students with both.

q: Table T(a, b) = (1,NULL), (2,3). What does SELECT SUM(a + b) FROM T return?
exp: a + b gives NULL for the first row and 5 for the second; SUM ignores NULLs, so the result is 5.

q: R(StudentID, CourseID, StudentName, Grade) has key (StudentID, CourseID). Which dependency causes a 2NF violation?
exp: StudentName depends on StudentID, which is only part of the key (a partial dependency), violating 2NF.

q: A cascading rollback occurs when
options: a transaction is rolled back after all its locks are released
the failure of one transaction forces the rollback of other transactions that read its uncommitted data
two transactions request the same lock
exp: If Ti aborts, any Tj that read Ti's uncommitted writes must also abort, possibly triggering a chain of rollbacks.

q: After a money transfer between two accounts, the combined balance of both accounts has changed. Which ACID property has been violated?
exp: Consistency requires transactions to take the database from one valid state to another; a changed total breaks the integrity rule that the sum stays the same.

q: Which is a typical characteristic of an OLAP system as compared with OLTP?
options: Complex analytical queries over large volumes of historical, aggregated data
Many short update transactions on current data
Very high number of concurrent writers
exp: OLAP supports decision-making with complex read-mostly queries over historical data, while OLTP handles many short transactions.
